opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's an intuition that as models get smarter, they'll become more alien and harder to understand. But I actually think the opposite may hold in important ways.

First, interpretability isn't something we do by hand. The early days were people staring at individual neurons. Now the field has moved toward unsupervised methods, like sparse autoencoders and other decomposition techniques, that pull out the concepts a model represents. Those methods scale with compute, just like the models do. So as we get more compute and better infrastructure, our ability to map a model's internals grows too.

Second, we can use AI to help interpret AI. A lot of the bottleneck has been human labor: labeling features, tracing circuits, forming hypotheses about what a mechanism does. More capable models are getting very good at exactly that kind of work. So the same progress that makes the subject models harder to understand also gives us better tools for understanding them. It's not a fixed human team racing an ever-faster target. Both sides are accelerating.

Third, there's some evidence that as models get more capable, their representations become cleaner and more structured. Smarter models seem to converge on more coherent, more human-relatable abstractions, because those abstractions actually reflect the structure of the world. A small, confused model can be messier to interpret than a large one that has really learned the concept.

And finally, there's just a strong incentive. Neural networks are the most important technology being built right now, and we deploy them in high-stakes settings without really understanding how they work. That's unusual for engineering. You wouldn't build a bridge or a power plant that way. Businesses and governments will need to debug these systems, steer them, and verify they're doing what we think. That demand pulls a lot of talent and resources into the field.

So I'm optimistic. It won't be automatic, and there are real open problems. But I think interpretability is fundamentally a scalable science, not a craft, and that's why I believe it can keep up.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help label features and form hypotheses, but does not clearly state that a language model infers what a latent concept represents.

r002.rationale: It says more capable AI models can help with interpretation, but does not specifically state that interpretation improves as the language models performing it become more capable.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest (Eric Ho): That's really the core bet of the whole field, and honestly, it's the question I get asked most. My answer is that I think interpretability can keep pace precisely because it's not a static technique we're applying to a moving target. The tools themselves are getting better alongside the models, and in some ways because of the models.

Let me unpack that a little. A few years ago, if you wanted to understand what a neural network was doing, you were basically staring at individual neurons and hoping they corresponded to something human-legible. That worked okay for vision models and small language models, but it broke down fast because of superposition, where a single neuron is doing five different jobs at once. So the field moved to things like sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning, which let you decompose activations into features that are actually monosemantic. That was a conceptual leap, not just an incremental improvement, and it was driven by the models getting harder to read.

The second thing is that we're increasingly able to use the models to help us interpret the models. Automated interpretability, where you have one model label and explain the features of another, scales in a way that human-in-the-loop analysis never could. Nobody is going to manually read millions of features. But a model can propose hypotheses, test them, and flag the ones that matter, and then a human comes in at the end to verify. So as the models get smarter, our interpretability assistants get smarter too. There's a kind of built-in ratchet there.

Now, I want to be honest about the risks. There's a version of this where the capability gap outruns our ability to verify what the assistant model is telling us, and then you're trusting the thing you're trying to audit. That's a real failure mode, and it's why I think you need the interpretability tools to be grounded in something mechanistic and checkable, not just a model saying "trust me, this feature means X." The verification has to bottom out in actual circuit-level evidence, ablations, causal interventions, things you can confirm independently.

And the third reason I'm optimistic is more structural. Intelligence doesn't make a system opaque in some fundamental sense. In a lot of cases, more capable models actually have cleaner, more abstract internal representations. The concepts are more crisply separated because the model needs them to be in order to generalize. So in some ways, a smarter model can be easier to interpret than a confused, mid-sized one that's using messy heuristics.

So the honest summary is: I don't think it's guaranteed, but the trajectory so far has been that every time models have gotten harder to understand, the field has found a new abstraction that catches up. And now we have a feedback loop where the models themselves accelerate that process. The job is to make sure that loop stays grounded in evidence we can independently verify. If we do that, I think we keep pace.

r001.rationale: It describes one model labeling and explaining another model’s features, which communicates using a model to infer what its learned features represent.

r002.rationale: It says interpretability assistants get smarter as the models get smarter, explicitly linking greater model capability to improved interpretation.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think it’s guaranteed, but one reason I’m optimistic is that the tools we use to understand models can get more intelligent too. We’re not limited to a human manually inspecting every neuron. We can use models to help generate hypotheses about what another model is doing, design experiments, and interpret the results.

The key is making sure those explanations are testable. If we think a particular mechanism drives a behavior, can we intervene on that mechanism and predict how the behavior changes? That gives us something stronger than a plausible story.

So the question isn’t just whether humans can keep up with increasingly intelligent models unaided. It’s whether increasingly capable tools, paired with careful experiments, can keep our understanding moving forward. I think there’s a reasonable path there, even though we still have to demonstrate that it works.

r001.rationale: The response says models can help generate hypotheses about another model’s behavior, but does not describe inferring what a latent concept represents.

r002.rationale: It says the models used as interpretability tools can become more intelligent and that increasingly capable tools can advance understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think it’s guaranteed, but I’m optimistic because the tools we use to understand models can improve alongside the models themselves. We don’t have to rely on a human manually inspecting every neuron. We can use AI to help identify patterns, propose explanations, and design experiments to test those explanations.

The crucial distinction is between getting a model to tell us a plausible story about what it’s doing and actually checking that story. If we think we’ve found a mechanism, can we intervene on it and predict how the model’s behavior will change? That gives us something more solid than an explanation that just sounds convincing.

So I think there’s a path for interpretability to keep pace, but it requires turning better AI capabilities into better measurement and verification tools. It won’t happen automatically.
